questions.stem: A 38 year old man has had type 1 diabetes since age 14. He attends his annual review and feels well. He has background retinopathy. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. Urine dipstick is negative for protein.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A raised ACR below the dipstick threshold in a long-standing diabetic with retinopathy is the first sign of diabetic nephropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Long duration of diabetes and microvascular disease elsewhere. Dipstick-negative but ACR raised means microalbuminuria.

elim: Causes lower urinary tract symptoms, not albuminuria; he has none.
Typically presents with visible haematuria after a sore throat in a young adult.
Causes heavy proteinuria with nephrotic syndrome; dipstick would be strongly positive.
Would give symptoms and leucocytes/nitrites, not isolated low-level albuminuria.

steps.x: B. Diabetic nephropathy (microalbuminuria stage). Microalbuminuria is the first sign and is often asymptomatic; dipstick misses it.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with type 2 diabetes for 20 years has 2 months of worsening ankle swelling and tiredness. Her HbA1c has been above 75 mmol/mol for years. She has laser-treated retinopathy. There is pitting oedema to the knees. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 158/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Long-standing poorly controlled diabetes with retinopathy, heavy albuminuria, oedema and low albumin is advanced diabetic nephropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Long duration and poor control are the key risk factors; retinopathy shows microvascular damage; oedema with low albumin shows protein loss.

elim: No breathlessness, orthopnoea or raised JVP; the urine and albumin findings point to the kidney.
No stigmata of liver disease or alcohol history; heavy proteinuria explains the low albumin.
Causes fatigue and non-pitting myxoedema, not heavy proteinuria.
Causes resistant hypertension and rising creatinine with little proteinuria.

steps.x: B. Diabetic nephropathy. Chronic hyperglycaemia damages glomeruli, giving proteinuria and falling function.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with type 2 diabetes has had microalbuminuria for 6 years but stopped his medication. He feels well. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg. Today his early morning urine albumin:creatinine ratio is 46 mg/mmol, confirmed on repeat.
questions.q: Which best describes the stage of his kidney disease?
questions.e: ACR at or above 30 mg/mmol is macroalbuminuria, the stage after microalbuminuria and before CKD.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes the stage of his kidney disease? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
The ACR has climbed past 30 mg/mmol, showing progression along the microalbuminuria to macroalbuminuria path.

elim: Microalbuminuria is ACR 3 to 29 mg/mmol; 46 is above this.
Needs haematuria, hypertension and oliguria with an active sediment, not isolated albuminuria.
Normal is ACR below 3 mg/mmol.
Defined by very low eGFR needing dialysis, not by an ACR value.

steps.x: B. Macroalbuminuria. ACR ≥3 is micro, ≥30 is macro; disease then progresses to CKD.

questions.stem: A practice nurse reviews the records of five patients with type 2 diabetes to decide who is at greatest risk of developing albuminuria. All have similar ages. Which feature in a patient's record most increases the risk of diabetic nephropathy?
questions.q: Which is the most likely risk factor?
questions.e: Hypertension, poor glycaemic control and long duration of diabetes are the risk factors for diabetic nephropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely risk factor? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
The question wants a recognised risk factor: diabetes itself, hypertension, poor control and duration.

elim: Not a recognised risk factor for diabetic kidney disease.
Sex is not one of the listed risk factors; hypertension is.
Irrelevant to glomerular damage.
Risk rises with LONG duration, not short.

steps.x: C. Poorly controlled hypertension. Hypertension drives intraglomerular pressure and is a key modifiable risk factor.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy (ACR 64 mg/mmol, eGFR 44 mL/min/1.73m²) asks what problem her kidney disease puts her most at risk of dying from. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day. Her total cholesterol is 6.1 mmol/L. Her BP is 146/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of death in this patient?
questions.e: Albuminuric CKD greatly increases cardiovascular risk, so most patients die of cardiovascular disease before reaching end-stage renal failure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of death in this patient? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Albuminuria plus smoking and raised cholesterol stack up cardiovascular risk.

elim: She has type 2 diabetes; DKA is not the main long-term threat.
Possible in advanced CKD, but her eGFR is moderate; cardiovascular disease dominates.
Not a complication of diabetic nephropathy.
Occurs only in end-stage disease without dialysis.

steps.x: C. Myocardial infarction. Cardiovascular disease is the major complication; hence statins and smoking cessation.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with diabetic nephropathy has 3 weeks of abdominal swelling and leg oedema. He does not drink alcohol. There is shifting dullness. His BP is 150/86 mmHg. Ascitic fluid is clear. Investigations: serum albumin 22 g/L (35–50), ascitic albumin 16 g/L, urine ACR 340 mg/mmol (<3).
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on ascitic fluid analysis?
questions.e: Protein loss in nephropathy causes low-SAAG ascites (<1.1 g/dL): serum albumin minus ascitic albumin is 0.6 g/dL here.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on ascitic fluid analysis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
22 − 16 = 6 g/L = 0.6 g/dL. Heavy albuminuria, not portal hypertension, explains the ascites.

elim: No weight loss or mass; clear fluid argues against malignancy.
This defines spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; he has no fever or pain.
A high gradient indicates portal hypertension, e.g. cirrhosis or heart failure.
Chylous ascites; the fluid is clear.

steps.x: D. Serum-ascites albumin gradient below 1.1 g/dL. Nephrotic-range protein loss gives a LOW SAAG; portal hypertension gives a high one.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has had type 1 diabetes for 18 years. She has no symptoms and no oedema. Her BP is 128/80 mmHg. Her ACR was 5.2 mg/mmol in March, 6.8 mg/mmol in May and 7.1 mg/mmol in July. Urine microscopy shows no red cells. Her eGFR is 92 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Persistent microalbuminuria (2 of 3 readings ≥3 mg/mmol over at least 3 months) in long-standing type 1 diabetes is early diabetic nephropathy, usually asymptomatic.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Three raised readings over 4 months with no symptoms and normal eGFR fits the earliest stage.

elim: Would usually show red cells or casts on microscopy.
Needs heavy proteinuria, oedema and hypoalbuminaemia.
Two of three ACR readings over 3 months are ≥3 mg/mmol, which is abnormal.
Presents with flank pain, haematuria or palpable kidneys, often with family history.

steps.x: A. Early diabetic nephropathy. Early disease is asymptomatic with microalbuminuria only.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with diabetic nephropathy has 2 weeks of nausea, itch and weakness. His BP is 168/96 mmHg. ECG shows peaked T waves (see item resources). Investigations: potassium 6.7 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), urea 32 mmol/L (2.5–7.8), eGFR 9 mL/min/1.73m² (>90).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: eGFR below 15 with uraemic symptoms and hyperkalaemia is end-stage renal failure from diabetic nephropathy; it needs urgent nephrology input.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Uraemic symptoms, hyperkalaemia and eGFR <15 mean the kidneys have failed.

elim: Would cause fever and loin pain; this is a gradual uraemic picture.
Can cause hyperkalaemia but with hypotension, not BP 168/96.
Needs ketonaemia and acidosis in a usually type 1 patient; uraemia explains this.
Follows muscle injury or immobility with raised CK; none here.

steps.x: D. End-stage renal failure. Worsening renal function with high potassium in a diabetic means advanced disease.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years notices her urine has become frothy and her rings feel tight. She has peripheral neuropathy. Her BP is 148/90 mmHg. There is pitting ankle oedema. Investigations: serum albumin 29 g/L (35–50), urine ACR 180 mg/mmol (<3), total cholesterol 7.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her oedema?
questions.e: Glomerular damage lets albumin leak into urine (frothy), lowering serum albumin and oncotic pressure, causing oedema.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her oedema? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Frothy urine and a high ACR show protein loss; low albumin explains the oedema.

elim: She takes no drug that causes ankle oedema in the stem; the urine finding explains it.
Would usually be unilateral with calf pain.
Non-pitting and localised, without proteinuria.
Expect raised JVP and breathlessness; albumin is low because of urinary loss.

steps.x: D. Proteinuria with low serum albumin. Low serum albumin and oedema are late features of diabetic nephropathy.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years and proliferative retinopathy has a renal biopsy because his creatinine rose faster than expected. Light microscopy shows round PAS-positive nodules of mesangial matrix at the periphery of the glomeruli.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions) is the classic histological finding of advanced diabetic nephropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Long-standing diabetes plus mesangial nodules on biopsy is the textbook lesion.

elim: Crescents in Bowman's space indicate rapidly progressive GN, not nodules.
Segmental scarring of some glomeruli, without nodules.
Shows 'spike and dome' basement membrane thickening, not nodules.
Light microscopy is normal.

steps.x: C. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodular glomerulosclerosis. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules = advanced diabetic nephropathy.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 11 years has an HbA1c of 82 mmol/mol (<48) and BP of 156/94 mmHg. He feels well and has no oedema. His urine dipstick is negative. His eGFR is 84 mL/min/1.73m². His ACR is 12 mg/mmol, and 14 mg/mmol two months later.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his ACR results?
questions.e: Poor glycaemic control and hypertension are risk factors; repeated microalbuminuria in an asymptomatic diabetic is the first sign of nephropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for his ACR results? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Two risk factors present; persistent ACR 3 to 29 with negative dipstick.

elim: Two raised samples make error unlikely, and contamination gives leucocytes/nitrites.
BP 156/94 with no end-organ symptoms is not an emergency.
Seen in adolescents; early morning samples are normal.
Causes a transient rise only; it would not persist on repeat.

steps.x: B. Early diabetic nephropathy. Microalbuminuria is the first sign; dipstick does not detect it.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes 6 years ago. She is well with an HbA1c of 54 mmol/mol. Her BP is 118/72 mmHg. She attends her annual diabetes review and asks which test checks her kidneys for early damage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate screening investigation?
questions.e: All diabetic patients have annual early morning urine ACR screening; it detects microalbuminuria, the first sign.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate screening investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Annual review in a diabetic; the earliest damage is microalbuminuria.

elim: Cumbersome and not used for routine annual screening.
Invasive; not a screening test.
Shows structure, not early glomerular leak.
Not sensitive enough to detect microalbuminuria.

steps.x: B. Early morning urine albumin:creatinine ratio. Annual early morning ACR for everyone with diabetes.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man with type 2 diabetes has an early morning urine albumin:creatinine ratio of 5 mg/mmol at his annual review. His previous ACR one year ago was 1.4 mg/mmol. He is asymptomatic. His BP is 136/84 mmHg. He is anxious to know whether he has kidney disease.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Repeat ACR twice within the next 3 months
questions.e: Persistent microalbuminuria needs 2 of 3 elevated readings over at least 3 months; one raised sample must be repeated.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
One new raised ACR. Exercise or infection can raise a single sample.

elim: Not needed; the diagnosis is made by persistent ACR.
A single raised reading is not enough.
Not indicated for early, unconfirmed microalbuminuria.
Too long; confirmation requires repeat samples within 3 months.

steps.x: E. Repeat ACR twice within the next 3 months. Confirm with 2 of 3 raised ACRs over at least 3 months.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with type 2 diabetes asks how her doctors will confirm whether she has diabetic nephropathy. Her BP is 132/80 mmHg. Her eGFR is 76 mL/min/1.73m². Her urine dipstick is negative. She has no haematuria and no family history of kidney disease.
questions.q: Which is the gold standard investigation for diagnosis?
questions.e: A persistently elevated ACR is the gold standard for diagnosing diabetic nephropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the gold standard investigation for diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Typical diabetic with no features of another kidney disease.

elim: Shows stones and structure, not glomerular disease.
Reserved for atypical cases; persistently raised ACR confirms the diagnosis.
Rises late, after albuminuria.
Used for nephritis, not diabetic nephropathy.

steps.x: B. Persistently raised urine albumin:creatinine ratio. Persistently raised ACR confirms it; biopsy only if atypical.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes 2 years ago. His mother asks when his kidney function blood test (eGFR) will first be checked as part of nephropathy screening. He is well, and his urine ACR is 0.8 mg/mmol. His BP is 112/68 mmHg.
questions.q: When should eGFR screening for nephropathy begin?
questions.e: In type 1 diabetes eGFR is checked after 5 years, because nephropathy takes years to develop; in type 2 it is checked at diagnosis.

steps.x: The question asks: When should eGFR screening for nephropathy begin? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Type 1, short duration. Onset of type 1 is known precisely.

elim: That is the rule for type 2 diabetes, which may have been present for years before diagnosis.
eGFR is part of routine screening, not only after albuminuria.
Early disease is asymptomatic; waiting misses it.
Screening is tied to diabetes duration, not a fixed age.

steps.x: A. 5 years after diagnosis. Type 1: eGFR after 5 years; type 2: at diagnosis. ACR annually for both.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with type 2 diabetes has persistent macroalbuminuria and is starting ramipril. His BP is 150/92 mmHg. His GP plans the baseline blood tests needed before and during treatment and to stage his kidney disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate set of blood tests?
questions.e: eGFR and U&Es assess renal function and potassium (needed for ACE inhibitors); lipids and HbA1c guide risk management.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate set of blood tests? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Needs renal function and potassium for the ACE inhibitor, plus cardiovascular and glycaemic risk.

elim: For vasculitis or Goodpasture's, not routine diabetic CKD.
Infection tests; not relevant.
Do not assess renal function or potassium.
For pancreatitis.

steps.x: E. U&Es, eGFR, lipids and HbA1c. Monitor ACR and eGFR regularly; check U&Es, lipids and HbA1c.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with diabetic nephropathy is on ramipril and dapagliflozin. Her eGFR is stable at 52 mL/min/1.73m². Her BP is 128/78 mmHg. Her ACR, previously 48 mg/mmol, has been 22 mg/mmol for a year.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring?
questions.e: Progression and response are monitored by regular ACR and eGFR; her ACR has fallen from macro- to microalbuminuria range on treatment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Treatment has worked; she still needs follow-up.

elim: Invasive and unnecessary for monitoring.
Does not track albuminuria or function.
Diabetic nephropathy needs lifelong monitoring.
Too insensitive to track ACR changes.

steps.x: D. Regular ACR and eGFR. Track disease by ACR and eGFR.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man with type 1 diabetes has persistent microalbuminuria with ACR 8 mg/mmol on three samples over 4 months. His BP is 128/78 mmHg. His HbA1c is 58 mmol/mol. He takes insulin only. His eGFR is 86 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: An ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is indicated for ACR ≥3 mg/mmol; it reduces proteinuria and protects the kidney while controlling BP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Confirmed microalbuminuria. BP is near target but ACR ≥3 alone is the indication.

elim: Lowers BP but does not reduce intraglomerular pressure or proteinuria like an ACE inhibitor.
Not first-line for albuminuria.
SGLT2 inhibitors are added in type 2 diabetes already on ACE inhibitor/ARB.
ACE inhibitor is indicated for ACR ≥3 even if BP is normal.

steps.x: E. Ramipril. ACE inhibitor/ARB for ACR ≥3 mg/mmol, regardless of BP.

questions.stem: A 55 year old Black African woman with type 2 diabetes and ACR 40 mg/mmol was started on lisinopril. Two weeks later she has a persistent dry cough that disturbs her sleep. Her BP is 138/84 mmHg. Her potassium is 4.8 mmol/L and eGFR is unchanged.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: ACE inhibitor cough is bradykinin-mediated; an ARB gives the same renal protection without it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Classic ACE inhibitor side effect in someone who still needs RAAS blockade.

elim: Leaves the cough untreated.
Treats the symptom, not the cause.
She needs RAAS blockade for albuminuria; an ARB avoids the cough.
Loses the renal protection of RAAS blockade.

steps.x: E. Switch to losartan. ACE inhibitor or ARB; switch to an ARB if cough.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD takes metformin and the maximum dose of ramipril. His BP is 128/76 mmHg. His eGFR is 48 mL/min/1.73m² and ACR is 52 mg/mmol. His HbA1c is 56 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: An SGLT2 inhibitor is added in type 2 diabetes with CKD already on maximal ACE inhibitor/ARB and ACR >30 mg/mmol; it reduces albuminuria and slows progression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Already on RAAS blockade, BP at target, ACR still above 30.

elim: Lowers glucose but has no renal protective effect.
Used when BP is above target; his BP is controlled.
Dual RAAS blockade increases hyperkalaemia and AKI risk.
Metformin can continue at eGFR 48.

steps.x: A. Add dapagliflozin. SGLT2 inhibitor next for type 2 with ACR >30 on ACE inhibitor/ARB.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and CKD takes maximum dose candesartan and empagliflozin. Her ACR is 85 mg/mmol and eGFR 39 mL/min/1.73m². Her clinic BP is 146/88 mmHg on two visits and home readings average 142/86 mmHg. Potassium is 4.9 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: No change; BP is at target
questions.e: With BP above the <130/80 target despite maximised ARB, a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide is added.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Maximised RAAS blockade, ACR above 70, BP over target.

elim: ACE inhibitor plus ARB is not recommended (hyperkalaemia, AKI).
Risky with potassium already 4.9 on an ARB.
Already at maximum dose.
Target with ACR >70 is <130/80; she is above it.

steps.x: A. Add indapamide. Target BP <130/80 with ACR >70; add a thiazide-like diuretic.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy started dapagliflozin 6 weeks ago. She now has vulval itching and a thick white discharge. Her BP is 126/78 mmHg. Her ACR has fallen and her eGFR is stable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria, predisposing to genital candidiasis, a recognised side effect.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
New SGLT2 inhibitor; itch plus thick white discharge is thrush.

elim: ACE inhibitor allergy causes angioedema, not discharge.
Gives thin grey fishy discharge, not thick white with itch.
Usually asymptomatic or causes bleeding and pain.
White skin plaques with itching but no discharge.

steps.x: E. Vaginal candidiasis from glycosuria. SGLT2 inhibitors: renal protection, but watch for vaginal candidiasis.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with type 2 diabetes and ACR 90 mg/mmol takes ramipril, dapagliflozin and atorvastatin. His home BP readings average 134/84 mmHg. His HbA1c is 52 mmol/mol. He asks what his BP target is.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate target blood pressure?
o: No target, as BP does not affect CKD
questions.e: For CKD with ACR >70 mg/mmol the target is <130/80 mmHg.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate target blood pressure? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Heavy albuminuria means the stricter target.

elim: Too strict; risks hypotension and AKI.
The general target; tighter control is needed with heavy albuminuria.
Target for over 80s without CKD.
BP control slows progression.

steps.x: B. Below 130/80 mmHg. ACR >70 → BP <130/80.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria takes ramipril. His BMI is 34 kg/m². He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and adds salt to meals. His BP is 136/84 mmHg. His QRISK3 is 18%. He is not on any lipid-lowering drug.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
questions.e: Long-term care includes statin therapy plus weight control, salt reduction and smoking cessation to cut cardiovascular and renal risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Several modifiable risks: smoking, salt, weight, lipids.

elim: Not recommended for primary prevention.
Lifestyle measures first; BMI 34 without other indications.
Not recommended; hyperkalaemia and AKI.
Not first-line lipid therapy; statins are.

steps.x: B. Atorvastatin and lifestyle advice. Statins plus lifestyle: weight, salt, smoking.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with diabetic nephropathy takes ramipril and spironolactone. She has 3 days of vomiting and feels weak. Her pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Investigations: potassium 7.0 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), creatinine 410 µmol/L (45–90), previously 180 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Discharge with repeat bloods in 1 week
IV calcium gluconate and urgent nephrology input
questions.e: Worsening renal function with high potassium in a diabetic indicates advanced disease; protect the heart and get urgent nephrology input.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Severe hyperkalaemia, rising creatinine, bradycardia.

elim: Life-threatening hyperkalaemia needs immediate treatment.
Worsens hyperkalaemia and renal function.
Too slow for potassium 7.0.
Inadequate and unsafe.

steps.x: C. IV calcium gluconate and urgent nephrology input. High potassium + worsening renal function = emergency.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with diabetic nephropathy takes ramipril and dapagliflozin. Over 9 months his eGFR has fallen from 28 to 19 mL/min/1.73m² and ACR is 320 mg/mmol. He feels tired. His BP is 132/80 mmHg. Potassium is 5.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Refer to nephrology to plan renal replacement therapy
questions.e: Advanced CKD needs nephrology referral; dialysis or transplant are considered as it progresses.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Falling eGFR towards end-stage; heavy proteinuria.

elim: Two ACE inhibitors is never appropriate.
Advanced CKD needs specialist planning.
No emergency indication now.
Not appropriate; medication still protects.

steps.x: C. Refer to nephrology to plan renal replacement therapy. Advanced CKD → nephrology, plan dialysis/transplant.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 15 years has persistent microalbuminuria. Her eGFR is higher than normal at 128 mL/min/1.73m². A medical student asks why albumin starts appearing in the urine at this stage.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Hyperfiltration with basement membrane and podocyte damage
questions.e: Chronic hyperglycaemia causes glomerular hyperfiltration, GBM thickening, mesangial expansion and podocyte loss, increasing protein permeability.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
High eGFR early on reflects hyperfiltration.

elim: That is anti-GBM disease.
Seen in glomerulonephritis.
Causes hydronephrosis, not albuminuria.
Causes glycosuria, not albuminuria.

steps.x: B. Hyperfiltration with basement membrane and podocyte damage. Hyperfiltration → GBM thickening → protein leak.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with type 2 diabetes and ACR 34 mg/mmol starts losartan. Two weeks later his creatinine has risen from 98 to 112 µmol/L. His BP is 132/80 mmHg. He has no symptoms. Three months later his ACR has fallen.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of the change?
o: Efferent arteriolar dilation reducing glomerular pressure
Inhibition of sodium reabsorption in the loop
questions.e: ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria; a small creatinine rise is expected.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism of the change? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Small creatinine rise and falling ACR after an ARB.

elim: Would increase glomerular pressure.
ARBs reduce aldosterone effects.
That is a loop diuretic.
Not suggested by a small rise.

steps.x: B. Efferent arteriolar dilation reducing glomerular pressure. ACE inhibitors/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and CKD starts dapagliflozin. Her eGFR falls slightly then stabilises and her ACR falls over 6 months. Her BP is 128/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of renal protection?
questions.e: SGLT2 inhibitors increase sodium delivery to the macula densa, causing afferent vasoconstriction and lower intraglomerular pressure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism of renal protection? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Small eGFR dip then stability is the haemodynamic effect.

elim: That is the action of loop diuretics such as furosemide.
That is ACE inhibitor/ARB action.
SGLT2 inhibitors do not affect insulin secretion.
Not the protective mechanism.

steps.x: E. Tubuloglomerular feedback causing afferent constriction. SGLT2i: sodium to macula densa → afferent constriction.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria asks why his doctor wants to block the renin-angiotensin system even though his BP is 126/78 mmHg. His eGFR is 74 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism being targeted?
questions.e: RAAS activation contributes to intraglomerular hypertension, driving protein leak even when systemic BP is normal.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism being targeted? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Normal systemic BP; the problem is inside the glomerulus.

elim: This lowers glomerular pressure; it is how SGLT2 inhibitors protect, not what RAAS blockade targets.
Seen in glomerulonephritis, not diabetic nephropathy.
The mechanism of myeloma kidney.
The target of SGLT2 inhibitors, not RAAS blockade.

steps.x: C. Intraglomerular hypertension from RAAS activation. RAAS → intraglomerular hypertension.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has an early morning urine albumin:creatinine ratio of 38 mg/mmol, confirmed on two further samples over 3 months. Her BP is 140/86 mmHg. Her eGFR is 70 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which describes her albuminuria?
questions.e: ACR ≥30 mg/mmol is macroalbuminuria.

steps.x: The question asks: Which describes her albuminuria? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Persistent ACR above 30.

elim: ACR 3 to 29 mg/mmol.
Not defined by ACR.
Normal ACR is <3 mg/mmol.
Seen in myeloma with light chains.

steps.x: A. Macroalbuminuria. ≥3 micro, ≥30 macro.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 30 years has had albuminuria for 12 years. His eGFR has fallen from 62 to 22 mL/min/1.73m² over 6 years. His BP is 142/84 mmHg. He has retinopathy and neuropathy. Urine microscopy is bland.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diabetic nephropathy progresses from microalbuminuria to macroalbuminuria to CKD.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Slow decline over years after long-standing albuminuria.

elim: Acute with drug trigger and rash.
Acute, not over 6 years.
Acute, with haematuria.
Cause colic and haematuria.

steps.x: D. Progressive diabetic nephropathy (CKD). Micro → macro → CKD → dialysis or transplant.
